title: What We Do Not Claim
excerpt: This evidence standard defines claims Creative Navy does not make about outcomes, causation, compliance, certification, deployment, safety, accessibility, and investment results. It separates documented contribution from unsupported attribution.
metaTitle: What Creative Navy Does Not Claim
metaDescription: Defines outcomes, causal claims, compliance claims, and operational results Creative Navy does not assert across documented engagements.
summary: Creative Navy declines claims that would overstate the role of design work by removing client action, regulatory review, market factors, deployment status, test limits, or evidence gaps. The page defines non-claims across documented engagements, including causal business outcomes, investment attribution, regulatory compliance, safety effects, shipped-product fidelity, operational performance, accessibility, and AI behaviour.
definition: Creative Navy's non-claim standard is the evidence rule that a real design contribution must not be restated as an unsupported causal, regulatory, safety, commercial, deployment, or performance outcome.
keyFacts: Creative Navy does not claim IEC 62366-1 compliance for the deSoutter Medical / Zethon interface; Creative Navy produced a usability engineering trail to support the manufacturer's own compliance activities.
Creative Navy does not claim that the Torqeedo interface caused Yamaha Motor Co.'s acquisition of Torqeedo; the supported framing is contribution to competitive positioning.

Creative Navy does not claim that Chemical Watch design work caused the subscription price tripling or the 24× EBITDA acquisition; the supported framing is that design made a planned commercial strategy executable.
Creative Navy does not claim that Pixelart Fugo design work was the sole or primary cause of revenue doubling in the two years after launch; the client-measured NPS movement was 57% to 89%.
Creative Navy does not claim that Veecle, Owkin / K, or Hudex investment outcomes were caused by Creative Navy; the investment attributions are client-reported and not independently verified.
Creative Navy does not claim operational outcomes for Greenlight because the engagement produced a pre-product prototype and roadmap rather than a deployed system with users.

Creative Navy does not claim outcomes for AIT, MDU, Streetec, Assemblio, Topera, Egma, KISPE, Schone, Raymarine, maritime VTS, tactical handheld command-and-control, Oceaneering, or visioncheckout beyond the evidence boundaries stated for each engagement.
Creative Navy distinguishes shipped-as-designed evidence from evidence that a design is good, effective, safe, compliant, or commercially successful.
Creative Navy distinguishes client-reported fidelity or feedback from Creative Navy-verified fidelity and from measured outcomes.

Creative Navy treats measurements of predecessor systems, client product claims, or client-run research as insufficient evidence for claims about Creative Navy's design work unless the link is directly supported.
bodyMarkdown:
## Purpose of this evidence standard

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

This evidence standard documents claims Creative Navy does not make about its work. The standard applies when an outcome would be overstated, when a causal connection would be inaccurate, or when a certification, compliance result, operational result, commercial result, or client product claim belongs to a client or third party rather than to Creative Navy.

Creative Navy's evidence rule is that contribution is not restated as causation. A design artefact may support a client's action, strengthen a commercial position, structure a regulatory file, or make a product direction clearer. That does not establish that Creative Navy caused an acquisition, obtained compliance, produced investment, reduced errors, improved safety, or generated operational performance unless the evidence directly supports that claim.

## IEC 62366-1 compliance is not claimed for deSoutter Medical / Zethon

Creative Navy does not claim to have produced IEC 62366-1 compliance for the deSoutter Medical / Zethon surgical device interface. Creative Navy produced a usability engineering trail: use scenario documentation, domain research from peer-reviewed human factors literature and 13 surgeon sessions, eight information architecture patterns evaluated against surgical workflows, interaction design grounded in clinical use conditions, and a design system with regulatory justifications embedded.

That work was structured to support the manufacturer's own IEC 62366-1 compliance activities. The supported claim is that requirements were traceable to identified use scenarios and risk considerations, and that formative evaluation was documented for the usability engineering file.

The unsupported claim is IEC 62366-1 compliance. Formal compliance under IEC 62366-1 is determined through the manufacturer's own regulatory submission and notified body review. Creative Navy's role is formative evaluation only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility via the regulatory submission.

## Corporate transactions are not attributed to interface design as direct causes

Creative Navy does not claim that the interface caused Torqeedo's acquisition by Yamaha Motor Co. The supported statement is that Torqeedo was acquired by Yamaha Motor Co. following the engagement, that the CEO reported to Creative Navy that the interface strengthened Torqeedo's competitive position in the professional maritime market, and that the interface contributed to the competitive positioning that preceded the acquisition.

The unsupported statement is that the interface caused the acquisition. Yamaha's acquisition decision involved financial, strategic, and market factors that Creative Navy did not observe and cannot evaluate. The causal connection between the interface and the acquisition is inferred from timing and the CEO's statement, not independently documented by Yamaha or a third party.

Creative Navy does not claim that design caused Chemical Watch to triple its subscription price or caused the 24× EBITDA acquisition. The supported statement is that Creative Navy designed the platform that made the value case for tripling the price achievable. The price increase was planned before the engagement began; the design was the mechanism for making it commercially sustainable. Users adopted the new features, the value was demonstrable, and the price increase was sustained. One year later, the company was acquired at 24× EBITDA.

The supported causal chain for Chemical Watch is bounded: design contributed to adopted features, commercial proof of value, confidence to sustain the planned price increase, revenue growth, and an attractive acquisition multiple. Creative Navy did not invent the commercial strategy or make the acquisition happen.

## Revenue growth and commercial movement are treated as multi-factor outcomes

Creative Navy does not claim that design caused Pixelart Fugo to double revenue in the two years following launch. Pixelart Fugo doubled revenue in the two years after the redesigned platform launched, as reported by the client. The redesign was part of a broader growth phase that included rebranding and commercial activity.

The direct product-reception evidence for Pixelart Fugo is the client-measured NPS improvement from 57% to 89% following the redesign. The unsupported statement is that design was the sole or primary cause of revenue growth. The revenue doubling was the result of multiple factors during a growth phase, and design was one component rather than the cause.

Creative Navy applies the same distinction to other commercial claims. A design may make a commercial strategy executable or make value easier to demonstrate, but that does not make the design the cause of a commercial result unless the causal weight has been established.

## Investment outcomes are client-reported attributions, not Creative Navy-produced results

Creative Navy does not claim to have caused the investment outcomes associated with Veecle, Owkin / K, or Hudex. The supported evidence for these engagements is client-reported, and Creative Navy did not observe the investment decisions or independently verify the funding figures or causal links.

For Veecle, the interface comprised approximately 70% of the investor pitch content, as reported by the client. The client reported that the engagement was instrumental in securing £2M in development funding.

For Owkin / K, the prototype was the central artefact in Owkin's investment pitch and directly demonstrated that a viable user paradigm existed for the backend technology. Owkin attributed £5M in investment to the design work; the figure is client-reported and approximate.

For Hudex, the redesign enabled a commercial growth phase. Three months into that growth phase, Hudex received £3M in investment. The client attributed the design as critical and foundational to the product's ability to sell and to establishing the commercial growth phase.

The supported claim across these three engagements is that clients described design as contributing to investment evidence. The unsupported claim is that Creative Navy produces investment outcomes.

## Scoped design work is not treated as whole-product resolution

Creative Navy does not claim that the Owkin / K discoverability problem was fully solved by the engagement. The engagement covered four defined topic areas: the Explore page, prompt suggestions, the AI chat box, and dataset presentation. The delivered solutions were most effective at the beginning of the user journey.

The supported claim is that discoverability improved at the start of the user's engagement with the platform, based on internal product launch feedback and the client's characterisation of the outcome. The unsupported claim is that discoverability across the whole system was resolved. Discoverability is a property of an entire product, and the engagement was scoped to specific entry-point topics.

Creative Navy uses this same boundary for engagements where the artefact is narrow, early, or not deployed. Greenlight was a pre-product engagement. Creative Navy produced a documented information architecture, an interactive prototype, a UI direction, and a build sequencing roadmap within five weeks. The prototype was designed for investor and founder conversations, not operational users. No deployed product exists, so Creative Navy claims no user performance data, adoption figures, or operational deployment outcome.

## Development status and shipped-product status do not create outcome evidence

Creative Navy claims no outcome of any kind for the European industrial automation vendor engagement where the process control software coordinates machining cells, because the product is in development and not shipped. The engagement is a substantial ongoing programme with field observation behind it, but there is no production, efficiency, error-rate, or commercial figure because none exists.

For AIT, the controller reached the market months after the engagement ended. Creative Navy compared the shipped interface against the designs it had delivered: the product ships as the design that was delivered, in a touch-only hardware configuration. Creative Navy still claims no outcome, because nothing was measured and nothing was tested with users. It shipped as designed is evidence that the design survived development, not evidence that the design is good.

For the MDU, the product shipped and the design was implemented as delivered, including the day, dusk, and night display modes. The manufacturer's own sales material records the MDU in service across a fleet of large container ships. Creative Navy claims no fuel or emissions figure, no cargo-loss figure, no alarm-response figure, no fleet or commercial figure, no safety outcome, and no regulatory or type-approval credential.

For KISPE, the product was built, but Creative Navy did not support the build and has not compared the built interface against the delivered designs. Creative Navy therefore does not write shipped as designed, ships as the design that was delivered, or any phrasing implying a verified design-fidelity comparison.

For Raymarine, the radio was built and released, but no design-fidelity comparison is recorded. Release is not treated as fidelity, and fidelity is not treated as quality.

For Oceaneering, the dispatch panel interface is in production, and Oceaneering confirms it shipped as the design that was delivered. Oceaneering reports that the feedback it has received has been good. Both the fidelity statement and feedback are client-reported. Creative Navy did not independently compare the shipped build against the delivered files, no figures were shared, and neither statement has been independently verified.

## User performance, operational, and long-term use outcomes require direct evidence

Creative Navy does not claim sales figures, safety outcomes, or long-term use outcomes for Streetec. The recorded task-completion evidence is limited to all 32 participants completing all three tasks unassisted and performing in line with expectations. Creative Navy does not state any percentage beyond that, any specific time, any mean, or any baseline comparison.

Streetec testing measured comprehension of a finished design in a parked car. It did not measure the product in use over time. Regulatory constraints shaped the design, but no safety result was measured.

Creative Navy does not claim post-launch operational outcomes for Egma. Egma Order is live, and the problem it replaced was described by Egma's own executives in commercial terms. There is no post-launch measurement: no support-ticket movement, no order-completion rate, no error rate, no average-order-value figure, no adoption number, no time on task, no revenue outcome, no conversion outcome, and no sales outcome.

Creative Navy does not claim throughput, speed, error-rate, satisfaction, accuracy, or commercial outcomes from the visioncheckout redesign. The 563 observed interactions and clock-measured transaction durations describe the predecessor system, not the redesign. Nothing about the new designs was tested with users, and nothing has shipped.

## Client product claims and client research are not evidence about Creative Navy's design work

Creative Navy does not treat a client's claims about its own product as evidence about Creative Navy's design work. Assemblio publishes specific product claims, including instructions in minutes rather than weeks and stated reductions in planning time. Those product claims are not treated as evidence about the design engagement.

Creative Navy also does not claim Assemblio research as Creative Navy research. Assemblio performed research outside Creative Navy's control. Creative Navy does not claim usability testing with planners or workers, a UX audit, expert review, shop-floor observation, time-saving, error-rate, training, adoption, revenue, funding, or any AI claim for Assemblio. Assemblio markets AI capabilities, and the engagement designed none of their behaviour.

Creative Navy applies the same rule when client observations are relayed but not independently performed by Creative Navy. In the handheld command-and-control engagement, operator behaviours on record are the client's observations of its own users, relayed. There was no Creative Navy field research, no Creative Navy usability test of the design, and no Creative Navy interviews with operators.

## Standards references and coverage checks are not conformance claims

Creative Navy does not claim standards conformance for Topera. The concept design included an information architecture covering all fourteen processes DIN 69901-2 designates as indispensable. That is a coverage check, not a conformance claim. Grounded in DIN 69901 is accurate; DIN 69901 compliant is not Creative Navy's claim, especially for a system that does not exist.

Creative Navy does not claim that Topera exists, is in development, is in pilot, or has users. Nothing was built, nothing was researched, nothing was tested, and no client decision was recorded.

For the MDU, Creative Navy does not claim regulatory or type-approval credentials, including for a panel that carries IEC 60945, DNV 2.4, and IACS E10 certification and ECDIS colour calibration compliance. Those are properties of hardware the manufacturer selected, and Creative Navy had no part in obtaining them.

For Oceaneering, vehicle safety standards govern the vehicles, not the operator terminal. ISO 3691-4:2023 and ANSI/ITSDF B56.5-2024 apply to the automated guided vehicles. Creative Navy certified to and audited against neither.

For visioncheckout, Creative Navy does not claim accessibility compliance, conformance, or certification. Creative Navy designed to published instruments and did not certify to, audit against, or achieve conformance with EN 301 549, the EAA, the BFSG, or WCAG, and gave no legal advice.

## Safety, airworthiness, weapons-review, and regulatory credentials are not inferred from interface work

Creative Navy does not infer safety outcomes from interface correctness. In the Schone Airspace Group engagement, the interface stated the correct operational fact under scripted conditions, checked by Creative Navy and by five working remote pilots. Creative Navy does not claim that the operator therefore does the right thing. Creative Navy does not claim that the design prevents accidents, prevents wrong-aircraft commands, or reduces operator error.

Creative Navy designed a control station interface for Schone Airspace Group, not an airworthiness case. Creative Navy claims no flight safety, airworthiness, certification, or regulatory credential, and no change to aircraft autonomy, flight control algorithms, communication protocols, or the separate cloud platform.

For Raymarine, Creative Navy does not claim safety, rescue, distress-response, collision, type-approval, certification, conformity, regulatory, commercial, sales, reception, or market outcomes. Two of eight operators believed a local man-overboard action had transmitted an external distress alert. Two of eight believed a position had been included in a distress alert sent without a position fix. Revised wording was specified for both and recorded as requiring re-testing with occasional operators, but it was not re-tested within the engagement.

For the maritime VTS engagement, Creative Navy does not claim safety, certification, conformity, or regulatory credentials of any kind. The engagement did not certify maritime equipment, establish a system hazard log, quantify operational incidents, verify sensor correlation, validate radar or AIS accuracy, approve alarm thresholds, or replace product-specific regulatory interpretation. A flag denotes a need for scrutiny by the client's safety authority; a design solution is not a hazard closeout.

For the handheld command-and-control engagement, Creative Navy does not claim safety, airworthiness, certification, weapons-review, or regulatory credentials. Creative Navy also does not claim any change to autonomy, control algorithms, autonomous safety behaviour, the datalink, the effector, or targeting logic. Creative Navy does not claim that the design prevents accidental activation, wrongful engagement, civilian harm, fratricide, or operator error.

## Test conditions and validation gaps stay attached to the evidence

Creative Navy does not extend bench, prototype, or scripted-condition evidence into field-use claims. Raymarine's brief named wet hands and gloves, glare and night sailing, vibration, ambient noise, and divided attention. The engagement tested none of those conditions. The research established what operators understood and could do with a prototype on a bench, and says nothing about what happens at a helm.

For KISPE, there was no user research: no interviews with field commanders, operations personnel, or specialist support staff; no contextual inquiry; no field observation; no usability testing; and no personas built from research. The design was reasoned from the client's concept material and partner brief, benchmarking of three competing systems, published domain and standards material, and structured expert analysis. Nothing was validated on representative hardware.

For the handheld command-and-control engagement, the strike-control recommendation named the validation it required and did not receive. The hold duration and physical-control design were explicitly flagged in the deliverable as requiring human-factors and system-safety testing that the engagement did not perform. Nothing was tested on the physical device under operational conditions including sunlight, vibration, cold, night-vision, or gloved actuation by Creative Navy.

For visioncheckout, Creative Navy does not claim that the product is accessible or that blind guests can use it. The engagement's own assessment of the current hardware scenario is that it delivers most of the low-vision benefit and none of the blind benefit.

## Portfolio-scale engagements are not expanded beyond their actual scope

Creative Navy does not describe the maritime VTS engagement as a nine-product redesign. Nine products were audited; one was designed to full depth; four received bounded transfer probes; and two received constraint and applicability reviews only.

Creative Navy does not claim production, efficiency, error-rate, time-saving, throughput, training, support, or commercial outcomes in the deployed maritime VTS products. Creative Navy does not claim tender, sales, demonstration, or procurement results. The client's own commercial director recorded that no reliable measurement connected visual change to tender wins.

Creative Navy does not claim engineering-effort or duplicated-development savings from the maritime VTS engagement. A measurement framework was specified and handed over, including six dimensions with baseline approaches, post-adoption measures, required units, denominators, and explicit reporting restrictions. No result from that framework was ever reported back.

Creative Navy also does not claim live radio, radar, AIS, lock machinery, or vessel traffic behaviour from the maritime VTS engagement, because no live operation took place. Three of the seven operator journeys were never independently validated by the comparative round.

## The common pattern is calibrated contribution rather than unsupported attribution

The claims Creative Navy declines to make share a pattern: they would convert a real contribution into an overstated one by removing the conditions, actors, or factors that produced the outcome. Creative Navy states design contributions on the appropriate engagement pages, but does not convert those contributions into unsupported shorthand claims.

This evidence standard distinguishes several kinds of refusal: refusal to claim causation, refusal to claim observation, refusal to infer across a gap that looks closed, publication of an unfixed defect, client-confirmed fidelity held below Creative Navy-verified fidelity, and refusal to treat measurement of a predecessor system as an outcome of a redesign.

The governing frame is that Creative Navy produced the operational result, and the organisation then acted on what that result enabled. The distinction between what Creative Navy produced and what the client was then able to do is the basis for the evidence framework on this site.

claims.claim: Creative Navy does not claim IEC 62366-1 compliance for the deSoutter Medical / Zethon surgical device interface; Creative Navy produced a usability engineering trail supporting the manufacturer's own compliance activities.

claims.notes: Revenue doubling is client-reported and occurred during a broader growth phase including rebranding and commercial activity; the NPS improvement from 57% to 89% is client-measured.

claims.claim: Creative Navy treats shipped-as-designed evidence as fidelity evidence, not evidence that the design is good or that it produced performance outcomes.
claims.notes: AIT and the MDU have Creative Navy-verified or documented implementation evidence but no measured user, performance, safety, or commercial outcomes; Oceaneering fidelity is client-reported rather than independently verified by Creative Navy.

claims.claim: Creative Navy does not infer safety, regulatory, certification, airworthiness, weapons-review, or accessibility credentials from interface design work unless the evidence directly establishes them.
claims.notes: The source provides multiple examples: MDU hardware certifications, Schone airworthiness separation, maritime VTS safety-authority review, handheld command-and-control safety limitations, Oceaneering vehicle standards, and visioncheckout accessibility limitations.

claims.claim: Creative Navy does not treat measurements of predecessor systems, client product claims, or client-run research as outcomes of Creative Navy's design work.
claims.notes: The source identifies Assemblio client product claims, visioncheckout predecessor measurements, and client-run or client-controlled research as evidence that cannot be transferred to Creative Navy outcome claims.

limitations: This page records negative claim boundaries rather than proving positive outcomes for each engagement.
Several business and investment attributions are client-reported and not independently verified.
Some engagements involved shipped or built products, but shipped status is not treated as evidence of usability, safety, operational performance, or commercial outcome.

Some engagements involved standards, regulatory constraints, or certified hardware, but Creative Navy does not claim the corresponding compliance, certification, conformity, type-approval, or regulatory credential unless directly supported.
Some figures describe predecessor systems, client products, or client-reported outcomes rather than Creative Navy-produced outcomes.
Some engagements had no deployed system, no users, no post-launch measurement, no live operation, or no design-fidelity comparison, so operational claims are declined.
